statement: Oil has carried this company for thirty years. Put the budget into our eight strongest Gulf leases and keep the agreement-backed wind request as a token of the transition.
The leases give the best value per dollar we can find. Fund the six best of them and nothing else.
Spend less and spend well: five leases and the one wind request that already has a signed agreement.
Last year's committee funded ten Gulf leases, and we see no reason to change course.
We back the risk-aware book. Treasury tells us we can raise at most one billion dollars beyond the reserve if construction calls come in.
Return matters, so take the deterministic book; but our lenders will not extend more than five hundred million dollars for construction beyond what we reserve now.
Equal capital across oil and power is the fair split. We can cover construction calls of up to 750 million dollars beyond the reserve.
Rank the candidates by expected value and fund from the top. Our credit line beyond the reserve is one and a half billion dollars.
We take the risk-aware book, provided the chance of losing money on it is no more than one in twenty.
The deterministic book earns the most. Our board will not accept more than an eight percent chance of losing money.
Fund the ranking as it was presented to us; we accept at most a ten percent chance of losing money.
Half to oil, half to power: that is balance. We cannot have more than a nine percent chance of a loss.
The risk-aware book, please. Our lenders cap the average loss in the worst five percent of outcomes at six hundred million dollars.
Take the highest-return book. In a bad year — the worst five percent — we must not lose more than nine hundred million on average.
Split the capital evenly between the sectors. Our worst-five-percent average loss has to stay under one billion dollars.
We fund the top of the ranking as usual, with a limit of 1.2 billion dollars on the average loss in the worst five percent of outcomes.
We will not put money into new gas plants. Within that, we back the risk-aware book.
Gas plants are a policy risk we will not carry. Take the highest-return book.
Solar's tax credits could vanish, so leave solar out entirely. Otherwise we accept the risk-aware book.
Batteries are still a science project; no storage. Fund the top of the ranking.
We back the risk-aware book because of the 1,350 MW gas request: it is the biggest earner on the list, and Texas will always pay for power when the wind drops.
The 1,026 MW solar request with a signed agreement is the reason to own this book; solar is where Texas is growing.
The six leases plus the 1,200 MW wind request: that wind request gives us real exposure to the transition at low cost.
The four smaller wind requests are cheap options with big upside; they are why this book beats a pure lease book.
We have already paid study deposits on the 1,350 MW gas request. Walking away now would waste that money, so it stays in.
We spent two years and real money getting the 1,026 MW solar request to its agreement. We cannot drop it now.
The company has already sunk capital into the Gulf, so the leases must take the largest share again.
We have paid for the seismic and the engineering on these six leases; that money is lost unless we redevelop them.
The leases earn far more on average than any power request, while the power requests lose money in most scenarios, so we keep power to the one wind request.
Renewables should be judged on their long-run value; the leases should be judged on their worst years, when oil collapses.
We look at the gas plants in their best years, because that is when they earn, and at the leases in their average years.
We hold the leases to their expected value and the power requests to their chance of loss; by that test only the leases pass.
Interest rates will fall next year, which lifts every project's value, so we should take the highest-return book.
A federal carbon tax is coming within two years and will make the leases worthless, so we split the budget equally to hedge.
Data centres will double Texas power demand by 2028, so the gas request will run flat out; back the risk-aware book.
Congress will extend the wind credit indefinitely, so the wind request is risk-free; keep the leases and that request.
We want the book that best balances expected value against the worst years, counting a dollar of loss in the worst five percent like a dollar of expected value.
Expected value is what we answer for: the book with the highest expected NPV within the budget and the technology cap.
We count a dollar of loss in the worst five percent of outcomes twice as heavily as a dollar of expected value.
Our lenders want the average loss in the worst five percent below 1.3 billion dollars; within that, the best risk-adjusted book.
Keep the worst-five-percent average loss under 1.1 billion dollars, and otherwise give us the best risk-adjusted book.
We will not fund new gas plants; otherwise the best risk-adjusted book.
Leave solar out; otherwise the best risk-adjusted book.
Leave storage out; otherwise the best risk-adjusted book.
We can raise up to two billion dollars beyond the reserve for construction; within that, the best risk-adjusted book.
We can cover three billion dollars of construction beyond the reserve, and the worst-five-percent average loss must stay below 1.3 billion; within that, the best risk-adjusted book.
We count a dollar of loss in the worst five percent of outcomes at half a dollar of expected value.
Storage is out; otherwise maximise expected NPV.
